raw_case_text:
A 41-year-old previously healthy female was admitted to a local hospital in Sri Lanka with a history of fever (38.9 C) associated with myalgia, arthralgia, headache, and abdominal pain for two days. She was diagnosed as DF with a positive Dengue NS 1 antigen test on day 3. She was managed for five days in the medical ward with close monitoring and cautious fluid management as per Sri Lankan national guideline on management of DF. Her condition remained stable throughout the initial five days without evidence of leaking or bleeding with a dropping but above 100 x 109/l platelet count. However, on the 6th day of fever, she was diagnosed to have entered the critical phase with clinical evidence of leaking and her packed cell volume (PCV) rose to 50. By this time, platelet count had also dropped to 57 x 109/l. During the same episode, her behavior was altered and she developed an episode of generalized tonic clonic convulsion that resolved spontaneously in two minutes. As her conscious level further deteriorated to a GCS of six, she was intubated and neuroprotective ventilation was commenced suspecting an intracranial haemorrhage. She was transferred to a tertiary-care unit, for CT brain and further specialized management. She progressed to a circulatory shock state despite several crystalloid and colloid boluses, as per guidelines. Meanwhile, serum calcium, sugar, and acidosis were corrected. Noradrenalin infusion was commenced to maintain mean arterial pressure more than 70 mmHg. Although the clinical picture was strongly suggestive of dengue haemorrhagic fever with leaking, there was no definite evidence of significant fluid collection in the lung bases or abdomen on ultrasound examination except for a mild gall bladder wall oedema. Possibility of a significant bleeding was less likely as her PCV and hemoglobin were rising. The bedside 2D echocardiogram reveled a low ejection fraction of 30-35% with globally hypokinetic left ventricle. T inversions and ST changes were evident on ECG and troponin I titre was elevated, all pointing towards a diagnosis of dengue myocarditis.
CT brain revealed an SAH of Fishers grade 3 with diffuse cerebral oedema. Because of the high risk of bleeding with a persistently low platelet count of 30-40 x 109/l and haemodynamic instability, decision was taken to manage conservatively without performing a decompressive craniotomy. Hence, neuroprotective ventilation was continued with the implementation of intracranial pressure-reducing strategies.
Due to SAH, platelet count needed to be maintained close to 100 x 109 mm3. Despite platelet transfusion, the platelet count remained below 40 x 109/l. There was no evidence in the blood picture to suggest disseminated intravascular coagulation or thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura. Hence, she was investigated on the line of HLH. Serum ferritin was 1500 mug/l, and LDH was 1247 mu/l. Bone marrow biopsy confirmed HLH. She was treated with immunoglobulin 20 g daily and high-dose dexamethasone as for HLH.
Even though she initially developed stage 1 acute kidney injury, on the second day of ICU admission, she developed polyuria (3.2 ml/kg/hr), with high serum osmolality and urinary sodium of 160 mmol/l. In the context of raised ICP following SAH, CDI was diagnosed along with urinary studies. Polyuria and hypernatremia further complicated the fluid management making bedside 2D echo and point-of-care ultrasound scanning a valuable tool to guide fluid therapy. Desmopressin nasal puffs were also used to control CDI.
Her condition continued to deteriorate despite the active multidisciplinary management. She expired on the third day of admission to the tertiary-care unit.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 41-year-old female presenting with fever (38.9 °C), myalgia, arthralgia, headache, and abdominal pain for two days.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 41-year-old previously healthy female was hospitalized with a 2-day history of high fever (38.9 °C), headache, body aches, and abdominal pain. She remained stable under guided fluid therapy until fever day 6, when she entered the critical phase with signs of plasma leakage and hemoconcentration. Simultaneously, she developed acute behavioral changes and a generalized tonic-clonic seizure lasting two minutes. Her conscious level rapidly deteriorated to GCS 6, necessitating emergent endotracheal intubation and neuroprotective mechanical ventilation for suspected intracranial hemorrhage. Following transfer to a tertiary ICU, she developed refractory circulatory shock, severe acute myocarditis, and central diabetes insipidus.
subjective.past_medical_history: Previously healthy; no prior medical comorbidities.
subjective.review_of_systems: Abdominal pain, myalgia, arthralgia, headache; no overt gastrointestinal or external bleeding.

objective.physical_examination: Day 6: Acute deterioration of consciousness (GCS 6), postictal state following generalized tonic-clonic convulsion. ICU admission: Circulatory shock requiring high-dose vasopressor support (norepinephrine); signs of increased intracranial pressure.
objective.routine_investigations: Day 6 labs: Packed cell volume (PCV) rose to 50% (severe hemoconcentration), platelet count dropped to 57 x 10^9/L (subsequently persistently low at 30-40 x 10^9/L despite platelet transfusions). Hemoglobin rising alongside PCV. Blood smear: No evidence of DIC or TTP. HLH workup: Serum ferritin 1,500 microg/L, LDH 1,247 U/L. Renal function: Initial stage 1 AKI; on day 2 of ICU, developed polyuria (3.2 mL/kg/h) with elevated serum osmolality and urinary sodium 160 mmol/L (central diabetes insipidus). Cardiac biomarkers: Elevated troponin I. ECG: T-wave inversions and ST-segment changes. Point-of-care ultrasound: Mild gallbladder wall edema without significant pleural effusion or ascites. Bedside 2D echocardiogram: Globally hypokinetic left ventricle with severely depressed ejection fraction (EF 30-35%), consistent with acute myocarditis.
objective.advanced_workup: Brain CT: Fisher grade 3 subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) with diffuse cerebral edema. Bone marrow biopsy: Confirmed hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Confirmed Dengue virus infection (severe dengue / dengue hemorrhagic fever with plasma leakage) complicated by catastrophic Fisher grade 3 subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH), diffuse cerebral edema, cardiogenic/circulatory shock secondary to acute dengue myocarditis, secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH), and central diabetes insipidus (CDI). Dengue confirmed by positive Dengue NS1 antigen on day 3. DIC, TTP, and major systemic occult bleeding were excluded.
Plan & Outcome: Neuroprotective mechanical ventilation and intracranial pressure-lowering strategies were instituted; decompressive craniotomy was withheld due to high surgical bleeding risk and refractory thrombocytopenia. Hemodynamics supported with targeted crystalloid/colloid boluses, electrolyte/acidosis correction, and norepinephrine infusion (targeting MAP > 70 mmHg). Repeated platelet transfusions were administered. HLH treated with intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG 20 g daily) and high-dose dexamethasone. CDI managed with desmopressin nasal puffs and echo-guided fluid titration. Despite aggressive multidisciplinary ICU care, her condition deteriorated, and she succumbed on the third day of tertiary ICU admission.
